transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, what brings me in is... I've just been living with this constant mix of guilt and fear and anger since my friend was killed. It just hasn't eased up the way everyone seemed to think it would. You know, people always say time heals all wounds, but I remember my grandmother used to say that time just makes the wounds older, not better. She had this beautiful rose garden, and she’d spend hours out there, just pruning and talking to the flowers. I tried gardening after I retired, I really did. I bought all the tools, the little gloves with the floral pattern, but the soil here is just so full of clay. You dig an inch and it's like hitting a brick wall. It’s funny how you plan for retirement and think you’ll have all this time for hobbies, but mostly I just sit in the living room and watch the neighbors walk their dogs. There's a golden retriever that comes by every morning at 8:15 sharp... but anyway, yeah, the guilt and the anger, it's just always there.
Do you find yourself repeatedly thinking about your friend's death in a way that feels intrusive or uncontrollable?

Oh, yes. Yes, I do. It’s like I have no say in the matter. Just... the beep of a crosswalk signal, or the loud growl of a delivery truck, or even just glancing at one of those little walking-tour maps they hand out to tourists. It suddenly puts the whole scene right back in my head so sharply. I can see my friend stepping off the curb before I can even stop the memory from happening. 

You know, speaking of those walking-tour maps, the city just redesigned them last spring. They used to be this nice, subtle pastel blue, but now they’re a terrible neon yellow. I suppose it’s so people don't lose them, but it’s just an absolute eyesore. I tried to take my niece on one of those historical tours when she visited from Ohio... oh, it must have been three years ago now. She’s a graphic designer, she went to state college for it, so she notices things like fonts and colors. She has two little boys now, twins, if you can believe it. They are just a handful, always getting into the kitchen cabinets. 

But anyway, what were we saying? Right, the thoughts. Yes, they just barge right in, and I'm right back there watching it happen all over again.
Do you find yourself avoiding certain places, activities, or people because they remind you of your friend's death?

Oh, absolutely. I go completely out of my way to avoid that intersection now. It's just too much. Actually, they've been doing a lot of roadwork around that part of town anyway, fixing the water mains or something. My neighbor Frank was complaining about his water pressure just last Tuesday. He’s the one with the golden retriever I mentioned earlier, the one I watch from the window! Such a sweet dog, his name is Barnaby. Frank feeds him those expensive grain-free kibbles, which I read an article about in a magazine at the dentist's office... they say it might not actually be good for their hearts, you know, the dogs' hearts. The dentist was talking about getting a dog, actually, a little poodle mix... 

But, oh, what was I saying? Right, avoiding things. Yes, I don't go near that intersection. And I’ve completely stopped signing up for most tours, or those neighborhood safety meetings. I just cannot bear the conversations, you know? They always seem to circle back to what happened there, and I just can't sit through it. The safety meetings used to be nice, though. They'd bring these little powdered donuts, the ones that get sugar all over your fingers... but no, I just stay home now.
Have you noticed any changes in your relationships with family or friends since your friend's death?

Well, yes, I suppose I have. I just don't feel connected to anyone anymore. Even when I sit with people I have known for years at the senior center, I feel completely separated from them. It's as if they are chatting on one side of a thick glass window and I am on the other, just watching their mouths move. 

We used to have such lovely times at the senior center, too. Every Thursday they do a watercolor class. I never thought I had any artistic talent, not like my sister—she used to paint these beautiful landscapes in oil, mostly of the coastline up in Maine where we used to spend our summers as children. The water there is so cold, even in August, but we’d swim until our lips turned blue. My mother would wrap us in these enormous, scratchy wool blankets... you don't really see blankets like that anymore, do you? Everything now is fleece or that microfiber material. I bought a fleece throw at the discount store last winter because my heating bill was just through the roof. The price of natural gas these days is criminal, honestly. I was talking to the mailman about it, he said his bill doubled... 

But anyway, what was I saying? Oh, right, my friends at the center. Yes, I just feel so distant from them now. I sit there while they paint or play cards, and I just feel like I'm a million miles away.
Has your feeling of being disconnected from others or your guilt and anger interfered with your daily activities or responsibilities?

Well, yes, I suppose it really has. I used to be so involved, you know? I was the one organizing the programs at the senior center, and I even managed the budgets for the volunteers. I was always good with numbers. My father was an accountant, actually, for a firm downtown that used to have this beautiful brass revolving door. They don't make doors like that anymore. Everything is automatic now, those sliding glass doors that always seem to open just a second too late so you feel like you're going to walk right into them. I did that once at the grocery store, just bumped my nose right against the glass. The manager came over, he was a nice young man, maybe twenty-two, wearing one of those green aprons... I think his name tag said 'Kevin.' He offered me a coupon for a free melon, but I don't really care for cantaloupe, it always leaves a funny aftertaste. 

But, oh, I'm sorry, what were we talking about? The activities, right. Yes, I just had to step back from all of it. The organizing, the budgets... I just can't keep up with it reliably anymore. And all those clubs I used to go to, the ones that gave my week some structure? I've just pulled away from them completely. I just can't seem to manage it now.
Have you experienced any significant changes in your mood, such as persistent depression, since your friend's death?

No, I wouldn't say I've been depressed, not exactly. I mean, I don't feel that heavy sadness people talk about. I remember my Aunt Clara, she had terrible depression after her husband passed away. She wouldn't leave the house for weeks, just sat in her parlor with the curtains drawn tight. Those heavy velvet curtains, they were a deep burgundy color, almost like a dark wine. You don't see velvet curtains much anymore, they gather so much dust. I spent a whole afternoon last spring just trying to dust the blinds in my living room. I bought one of those special tools from a catalog, the ones with the microfiber fingers? It looked so clever on the page, but honestly, it just pushed the dust from one slat to the next. The catalog had all sorts of gadgets, like a little device to slice strawberries perfectly even... my granddaughter loves strawberries, but only if they're cut up. She won't eat them whole, says the seeds look like little bugs. Children have such funny ideas, don't they? 

But... what was the question? Oh, my mood. No, no persistent depression. Just... well, just what we've been talking about, really.
Do you try to push away or avoid thoughts and memories of your friend's death when they come to mind?

Well, yes, I suppose I do. I mean, I go completely out of my way to avoid that intersection now. I just can't drive through it. I actually take the long way around by the old elementary school, the one with the brick facade. They built that school back in the fifties, I think. My brother went there, and he used to complain about the radiator clanking all winter. Those old steam radiators, they make such a racket, like someone hitting a pipe with a wrench. My apartment building had them when I first moved to the city. The super, Mr. Henderson, he was always down in the basement tinkering with the boiler. He had this enormous set of keys that jingled whenever he walked down the hall. You could hear him coming from three floors away. I always wondered why he needed so many keys. I only have three on my ring—house, car, and the little one for my safety deposit box. Though I hardly ever go to the bank anymore, everything is online. My nephew set up the app on my phone, but the buttons are so small, I always end up pressing the wrong thing...

Oh, dear, I've wandered off again, haven't I? What were you asking about? Oh, right, avoiding things. Yes, the intersection, definitely. And I've stopped signing up for most of the senior center tours or those community safety meetings, too. I just cannot bear it when the conversations circle back to what happened there. I just... I can't listen to it.
Have you experienced any significant distress or impairment in social, occupational, or other important areas of functioning since your friend's death?

Well, yes, I suppose it's like I mentioned before. It's really taken a toll on my routine. I've had to step completely back from organizing the programs at the senior center, and I gave up managing the volunteer budgets. I just can't keep up with it reliably anymore. It's a shame, really, because I used to love balancing those ledgers. I had this beautiful fountain pen I used just for the final numbers, a Parker pen, gold-nibbed. My husband gave it to me for our twentieth anniversary. We went to this lovely Italian restaurant to celebrate, the one with the red checkered tablecloths and the candles in the Chianti bottles. They served the most wonderful veal scallopini. I tried to make it at home once, but I couldn't get the sauce quite right. The recipe called for capers, and I always buy the ones packed in salt instead of brine, they have a much better flavor if you rinse them properly. My neighbor, Mrs. Gable, she puts capers in her potato salad, which I think is a bit strange. Potato salad should just have celery and maybe a little hard-boiled egg, don't you think? 

But... oh, goodness, I'm rambling again. I'm sorry. You were asking about how it's affected my life, right? Yes, so besides the budgets, I've just pulled away from all the clubs and activities that used to give my week some structure. I just can't seem to manage being around all of that right now.
Do you think the guilt, fear, and anger you're experiencing are directly related to your friend's death or is it more about something else that's been bothering you?

Oh, no, it's definitely about what happened to her. In fact, that's really what brings me in to see you. I have just been living with this constant mix of guilt, and fear, and anger ever since my friend was killed, and it hasn't eased up the way everyone seemed to think it would. People kept telling me, 'Time heals all wounds,' which is exactly what my grandmother used to cross-stitch on her decorative pillows. She made the most beautiful embroidered pillows, always with little floral borders. She had this wooden hoop she’d hold in her lap while she watched her afternoon stories on the television. As the World Turns, I think it was. Or maybe Days of Our Lives. I remember the theme song had this very dramatic organ music. I actually took organ lessons for a few years at our church, but my teacher, Mrs. Gantry, used to tap my knuckles with a pencil if my wrists dipped too low. Can you imagine doing that to a child today? The parents would be absolutely furious! My niece is a second-grade teacher, and she says they aren't even allowed to use red ink on grading papers anymore because it's considered too aggressive. They have to use purple or green. Green is a very soothing color, though. I painted my kitchen a soft sage green last spring, and it really brightens up the space when the morning sun comes in... 

Oh, dear me. I've completely lost the thread again, haven't I? I am so sorry. You were asking about the feelings. But yes, to answer your question, the anger and the fear and everything... it's all directly tied to her death. It's not about anything else.
Do you have difficulty remembering important parts of what happened when your friend was killed?

Well, no, I don't think so. I remember it all, unfortunately. I remember the sound of the tires, and the way the light was hitting the pavement... it had just rained, you see, so the street was very slick and shiny. I always hated driving in the rain, even when I was younger. My first car was this little blue Datsun, and the windshield wipers were absolutely terrible. They didn't really clear the water, they just sort of smeared it around in these big arcs. I had to pull over under an overpass once during a thunderstorm because I couldn't see a thing. There was a stray dog under there, too, a scruffy terrier mix. I tried to coax him over with a piece of a ham sandwich I had in my purse, but he was too frightened. I always felt bad about leaving him there, but the storm passed and I had to get to my shift at the library. I worked in the periodicals section back then, organizing all the magazines and newspapers. We used to get the Sunday New York Times, and it was so thick, it took up half a shelf on its own. The crossword puzzle was always my favorite part. I still do it every Sunday, though I have to use a magnifying glass now. My eyes just aren't what they used to be. I went to the optometrist last month, Dr. Chen, and he said... 

Oh, goodness, I'm doing it again, aren't I? I just start talking and my mind goes a mile a minute. I apologize. What was the question? Oh, remembering what happened. Yes, I remember it very clearly. Too clearly, really. I haven't forgotten any of it.
Do you ever feel like you're outside of your body watching yourself when you're reminded of your friend's death?

Outside of my body? Oh, no, I don't think I've ever felt anything like that. If anything, I feel very much stuck inside my body, especially lately with the weather turning. My knees just ache terribly when the barometer drops. I've been trying to take that glucosamine supplement my sister-in-law, Martha, recommended. She absolutely swears by it, but then again, she also wears one of those magnetic copper bracelets. She bought it at this lovely little craft fair in Sedona when she went to visit her daughter. Sedona is supposed to be just stunning, with all those red rocks and the vortexes, or whatever they call them. My husband and I always talked about taking a trip out West to see the Grand Canyon and all of that. We thought about renting an RV, but I just couldn't imagine sleeping in one of those tiny little beds. We used to have a pop-up camper when the children were small, and the mattresses were practically paper-thin. I remember one summer we went up to the state park, and a raccoon actually got into our cooler because my husband forgot to latch it properly. He had packed all these expensive artisan cheeses from that little deli on Main Street... 

Oh, for heaven's sake, there I go again. I am so sorry, doctor. My mind just wanders right off the path. But no, to answer your question, I don't feel like I'm watching myself from the outside. I'm just... here.
Do you find yourself trying to avoid thinking about your friend's death or things that remind you of it?

Yes, I do. I absolutely do. I go completely out of my way to avoid that intersection now. I just can't stomach being near it. And I've actually stopped signing up for most of my usual tours, and even the neighborhood safety meetings, because I just cannot bear it when the conversations circle back to what happened there. People always want to talk about safety after an accident, don't they? They get so worked up about crosswalks and speed limits. Which reminds me, they just put in a new four-way stop sign near my grocery store, the one over on Elm Street. It used to be a yield sign, and nobody ever actually yielded. My neighbor, Mr. Henderson, backed right into a delivery truck there last Thanksgiving. He was bringing home a fresh turkey from that farm out in the county—the one where they let the birds roam around in the pasture. Free-range, I think they call it. My mother always said a free-range bird makes a tougher roast, but I think it's all in how you baste it. She had this wonderful baster with a little rubber bulb on the end that she kept for forty years. It was cracked, but she refused to throw it away. She was like that with everything, really. She grew up during the Depression, you see, so nothing was ever wasted. She even saved the string from bakery boxes and rolled it up into a giant ball...

Oh, dear. I've done it again. I'm so sorry, doctor, I just start talking and my brain just takes a left turn. But yes, I do avoid things. The intersection, the meetings... I just try to stay away from anything that makes me think about it.
Do you try to push away or avoid thoughts and memories of your friend's death when they come to your mind?

Well, yes, I suppose I do. When the thoughts pop up, I try to just push them right out of my head. Just... shove them aside. It's like I was saying before about the intersection, I go completely out of my way to avoid driving past it now, and I've stopped going to the safety meetings and the tours because people always want to talk about it. It's just too much. I'd rather think about anything else. Like my garden, for instance. I've been trying to get my hydrangeas to bloom blue this year, but the soil here is just so alkaline. You have to add aluminum sulfate, you know, to lower the pH. My grandmother had the most spectacular blue hydrangeas lining her entire front porch. She lived in this beautiful old Victorian house with a wrap-around veranda. We used to sit out there on warm summer evenings and drink iced tea with fresh mint from her herb garden. She had a little patch of mint that just grew like a weed, took over half the flowerbed. Mint is very invasive, you have to be careful where you plant it, or it will just strangle everything else... 

Oh, goodness me. I've completely lost the thread again, haven't I? I'm so sorry, doctor. What was I saying? Oh, right, pushing the thoughts away. Yes, I do try to avoid thinking about it whenever I can. It's just easier that way.
Have you experienced any other stressful events or significant changes in your life around the same time as your friend's death?

No, I don't think so. Everything else was pretty much just... normal. Just the usual day-to-day things. Well, I suppose our water heater did break right around that same time, which was certainly a nuisance, but I wouldn't call it a major life change. It started leaking all over the basement floor, right onto these old cardboard boxes I've been meaning to sort through for years. You know how it is, you save things thinking you'll make a scrapbook one day. I had all the children's elementary school art projects in there. Macaroni necklaces and those little handprint turkeys they make for Thanksgiving. It's a shame how macaroni just attracts weevils if you keep it too long in a damp place. I remember my mother opened a box of elbow pasta once back in the seventies and a whole swarm of little bugs just fluttered right out. She was absolutely mortified because the vicar was over for Sunday supper. She ended up having to make a potato salad instead at the last minute, using those tiny red potatoes she grew out by the back fence. She always said the secret to a truly good potato salad was a dash of celery seed and just a tiny spoonful of sweet relish... 

Oh, heavens to Betsy. Listen to me rattling on about potato salad. I am so sorry, doctor, I've done it again. You asked about stressful events, didn't you? No, aside from the water heater acting up, there was nothing else going on. Just what happened to my friend.

Do you think your feelings of guilt, fear, and anger would improve if the circumstances surrounding your friend's death were to change in some way, such as finding out more information about what happened?

Well, I really don't know if having more information would change anything at this point. Because what brings me in is that I have been living with this constant, heavy mix of guilt, fear, and anger ever since my friend was killed, and it just has not eased the way everyone seemed to think it would. People kept telling me that time heals all wounds, and they kept giving me all these self-help books. My sister-in-law, Martha, gave me this enormous hardcover book about navigating loss. She buys absolutely everything that gets recommended on those morning talk shows. Martha has always been a bit of a busybody, bless her heart. She actually reorganized my entire spice cabinet while I was out at an appointment once. She alphabetized everything! Who alphabetizes spices? I couldn't find the cumin for three weeks. I was trying to make my famous chili for the neighborhood potluck, and I had to substitute with extra chili powder, which made it far too spicy for Mr. Gable from down the street. He has a very delicate stomach, you know. Ulcers, I think. He told me he has to drink a small glass of milk before every meal just to coat his stomach lining. My uncle Arthur had ulcers back in the eighties, and he swore by a spoonful of raw local honey every morning. He used to get it from a man who kept bees out behind the old middle school... 

Oh, goodness gracious. I am so sorry, doctor. I've completely lost the plot again, haven't I? Bees and spices... what on earth. But to go back to what you were asking... I just don't know if knowing more about what happened would fix how I'm feeling. The guilt and the anger are just always there, and they haven't faded at all like people promised they would.
How long have you been experiencing these feelings of guilt, fear, and anger since your friend's death?

Well, it's been going on ever since it happened. Since my friend was killed on that walking tour. That was about two years and three months ago now. It was early autumn, I remember, because the leaves were just starting to turn that lovely golden color on the maple trees down by the park. I've always loved autumn. It's my favorite season. The crisp air, the smell of woodsmoke... My grandfather used to have a little cabin up by the lake, and we would go there every October. He had this old cast-iron woodstove in the center of the room, and he would roast chestnuts on top of it. Real chestnuts, you know, not the kind you buy in a jar. You have to score them with a little 'X' before you roast them, otherwise they explode. I forgot to do that once when I was trying to make them for a holiday party, and one popped right out of the oven and nearly hit the cat! Oh, poor Mr. Whiskers, he was a Maine Coon, you know, absolutely enormous. He weighed almost twenty pounds and had tufts of fur on the tips of his ears like a lynx. He was terrified of loud noises, though. Whenever there was a thunderstorm, he would hide under the guest bed for hours. We had to coax him out with little pieces of canned tuna. Not the kind in oil, mind you, only the kind in spring water...

Oh, dear me. I'm doing it again, aren't I? I am so, so sorry, doctor. I just start talking and my brain just wanders right off down the garden path. You asked how long it's been. Yes, it's been about two years and three months since the walking tour. That's how long I've been feeling this way.
Have your symptoms of guilt, fear, and anger lasted for more than 6 months since your friend's death?

Well, yes, doctor. Like I was just saying a moment ago, this has been going on since my friend was killed on that walking tour about two years and three months ago. So that is certainly much longer than six months. 

Six months... you know, my granddaughter, Emily, just celebrated her six-month anniversary at her new job. She works at a bakery downtown. They make the most wonderful sourdough bread. Real sourdough, the kind where they feed the starter every single day. Emily says her boss named their sourdough starter Seymour. Isn't that a funny name for yeast? It reminds me of that old movie, the one with the giant singing plant. Little Shop of Horrors, I think it was called. My husband and I saw that at a drive-in theater back when drive-ins were still a thing. We had a baby blue Ford Falcon. The seats were vinyl, and in the summer, if you wore shorts, your legs would stick right to them and you would have to just peel yourself off...

Oh, for heaven's sake. Look at me, talking about vinyl car seats and singing plants. I am so sorry, doctor, my mind is just a sieve today. I really must try harder to focus. But yes, to answer your question, it has been much longer than six months. Like I said, it has been over two years.
Have your symptoms of guilt, fear, and anger been present every day since your friend's death?

Well, yes, it really has been every single day. That's actually what brings me in, doctor. I have just been living with this constant, heavy mix of guilt and fear and anger ever since my friend was killed, and it just hasn't eased up the way everyone seemed to think it would. Every day, it's just there. 

Every day... you know, I try to keep a routine every day, I really do. My doctor—my general practitioner, Dr. Evans—told me that having a daily routine is very important for people my age. He suggested I take up water aerobics. I tried it, I really did, but the chlorine in the pool at the YMCA just wreaks havoc on my skin. It gets so terribly dry and itchy. I bought this special lotion, it has oatmeal in it, I think. Aveeno, maybe? The bottle has a green pump. My daughter uses it for her youngest, little Tommy, because he has eczema. Oh, the poor dear, he gets these red patches on the back of his knees and inside his elbows. They tried everything—hydrocortisone, coconut oil, even some sort of special soap made from goat's milk that my daughter ordered off the internet. It came wrapped in brown paper tied with twine, very rustic looking. The woman who makes it lives on a farm in Vermont and she names all her goats...

Oh, good grief. Goat soap. I am so sorry, doctor. I've done it again, haven't I? I just can't seem to keep my thoughts in a straight line today. I apologize. But yes, to go back to what you asked, the feelings are there every day. It's a constant thing.
Have your symptoms of guilt, fear, and anger been present for at least 6 months but less than 2 years?

Well, no, doctor, not less than two years. Like I mentioned, it's been about two years and three months since the walking tour when my friend was killed. So it's been longer than that two-year mark. 

Two years... goodness, time really does fly, doesn't it? It feels like just yesterday I was renewing my passport. They make you take a new photo every ten years, and let me tell you, the lighting at the post office is just dreadful. It washes you out completely. I wore a lovely peach-colored blouse, thinking it would give me a bit of color, but I still looked like a ghost. My sister, Brenda, she always manages to look wonderful in her photos. She has this trick where she tilts her chin down just a fraction. She read about it in a magazine at the dentist's office. Speaking of the dentist, I need to call Dr. Miller's office. They sent me a reminder card in the mail, one of those oversized postcards with a cartoon tooth holding a toothbrush. It's so silly, but I suppose it catches your eye. The mail carrier, Jerry, he always laughs when he delivers them. Jerry is such a nice young man, he just had his first baby. A little girl, they named her Hazel. I knitted a tiny pink cardigan for her, with little pearl buttons down the front...

Oh, my goodness. I am so sorry, doctor. Knitting cardigans and passport photos... I am completely off track again. I don't know why I keep doing this. But to answer your question, no, it hasn't been less than two years. It's been two years and three months.
Have your symptoms of guilt, fear, and anger been present for more than 2 years?

Well, yes, doctor. Like I was just saying, this has been going on since my friend was killed on that walking tour about two years and three months ago. So, yes, definitely more than two years. 

More than two years... you know, my neighbor, Mrs. Gable, she's been trying to get her hydrangeas to bloom for more than two years. She planted them right by her front porch, beautiful big bushes, but they just won't produce any flowers. She's tried everything—coffee grounds, eggshells, even some special fertilizer she ordered from a catalog that smelled absolutely awful. It smelled like fish, if you can believe it. My cat, Barnaby, he went absolutely wild over the smell. He sat by the fence for three days straight, just sniffing the air. Barnaby is an orange tabby, you know. They say orange cats have very distinct personalities. He certainly does. He insists on drinking his water out of a human glass. If I put a bowl down for him, he just stares at it, then stares at me, like I've insulted him. I had to buy a set of those heavy-bottomed tumblers just so he wouldn't knock them over. I found them at a garage sale down the street. The woman having the sale had the most extensive collection of vintage salt and pepper shakers...

Oh, for pity's sake. Salt and pepper shakers and cats. I am so sorry, doctor. I am just talking in circles today, aren't I? I don't mean to waste your time. But yes, to answer your question, it has been more than two years. Two years and three months, to be exact.

Two years... goodness, time really does fly, doesn't it? It feels like just yesterday I was renewing my passport. They make you take a new photo every ten years, and let me tell you, the lighting at the post office is just dreadful. It washes you out completely. I wore a lovely peach-colored blouse, thinking it would give me a bit of color, but I still looked like a ghost. My sister, Brenda, she always manages to look wonderful in her photos. She has this trick where she tilts her chin down just a fraction. She read about it in a magazine at the dentist's office. Speaking of the dentist, I need to call Dr. Miller's office. They sent me a reminder card in the mail, one of those oversized postcards with a cartoon tooth holding a toothbrush. It's so silly, but I suppose it catches your eye. The mail carrier, Jerry, he always laughs when he delivers them. Jerry is such a nice young man, he just had his first baby. A little girl, they named her Hazel. I knitted a tiny pink cardigan for her, with little pearl buttons down the front...

Oh, my goodness. I am so sorry, doctor. Knitting cardigans and passport photos... I am completely off track again. I don't know why I keep doing this. But to answer your question, no, it hasn't been less than two years. It's been two years and three months.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's symptoms meet the duration criteria for PTSD
doctor.question: Have your symptoms of guilt, fear, and anger been present for more than 2 years?

patient.answer:
Well, yes, doctor. Like I was just saying, this has been going on since my friend was killed on that walking tour about two years and three months ago. So, yes, definitely more than two years. 

More than two years... you know, my neighbor, Mrs. Gable, she's been trying to get her hydrangeas to bloom for more than two years. She planted them right by her front porch, beautiful big bushes, but they just won't produce any flowers. She's tried everything—coffee grounds, eggshells, even some special fertilizer she ordered from a catalog that smelled absolutely awful. It smelled like fish, if you can believe it. My cat, Barnaby, he went absolutely wild over the smell. He sat by the fence for three days straight, just sniffing the air. Barnaby is an orange tabby, you know. They say orange cats have very distinct personalities. He certainly does. He insists on drinking his water out of a human glass. If I put a bowl down for him, he just stares at it, then stares at me, like I've insulted him. I had to buy a set of those heavy-bottomed tumblers just so he wouldn't knock them over. I found them at a garage sale down the street. The woman having the sale had the most extensive collection of vintage salt and pepper shakers...

Oh, for pity's sake. Salt and pepper shakers and cats. I am so sorry, doctor. I am just talking in circles today, aren't I? I don't mean to waste your time. But yes, to answer your question, it has been more than two years. Two years and three months, to be exact.
